summary: Subscriber Q&A. The main item explains why Democrats led the generic ballot by only 5.7 points in April 2026 despite Trump's 39.3 percent approval. Silver's answer: the number fits the historical trendline; registered-voter polls miss midterm enthusiasm gaps; the generic ballot is noisy and needs conservative smoothing; the opposition party tends to gain a point or two from April to November; and FLIPR uses presidential approval as a prior. It also announces the PELE soccer model and a June-July 2026 launch for the midterm model, and closes with baseball challenge game theory.

findings.statement: Generic ballot polls are 'bouncier' than other polling series, with little herding, possibly because the question is abstract and wording-sensitive and pollsters do not expect to be judged on it. Silver Bulletin therefore uses a more conservative smoothing setting for the generic ballot average, while its presidential approval average is tuned to react quickly.
findings.rationale: Curb noise in a bouncy series.
findings.evidence_quote: we’ve found that you need to use a more conservative setting for the generic ballot than for other sorts of polling averages to curb this bouncy tendency.

findings.statement: The midterm model uses presidential approval as a 'prior' for the national environment alongside the generic ballot, because approval contains information the generic ballot misses, even if it is not more predictive on its own.
findings.evidence_quote: And indeed, our model uses presidential approval as a “prior”.

findings.statement: The opposition party tends to gain a point or two on the generic ballot between April and November of a midterm year, measured against the eventual House popular vote. Silver calls the series noisy.

quantities.name: typical opposition gain April to November
quantities.context: generic ballot vs. eventual House popular vote

findings.evidence_quote: the opposition party tends to gain a point or two on the generic ballot between April and November

findings.statement: Historically the generic ballot has asymmetrically overrated Democrats at this stage of the cycle, possibly because Republicans used to have the more turnout-prone coalition. That may no longer hold: in 2022 the generic ballot was about spot-on at the equivalent point.
findings.evidence_quote: there’s been an asymmetric historical tendency for the generic ballot to overrate Democrats at this stage.

findings.statement: Early-cycle generic ballot polls mostly sample registered voters or all adults, so they miss midterm enthusiasm gaps that likely-voter screens capture. Silver expects the switch to likely-voter screens to favor Democrats in 2026, because the opposition party is usually more enthusiastic and the Democrats' college-educated coalition turns out heavily in non-presidential elections.
findings.evidence_quote: generic ballot polls at this point in the cycle are usually based on polls of registered voters or all adults — not likely voters

findings.statement: Plotted against presidential approval, the April 2026 generic ballot (D+5.7 with Trump approval at 39.3 percent) sits right on the recent trendline. Comparable points: D+7.6 in April 2018 and D+11.4 on April 21, 2006 under George W. Bush, the only president among the past nine midterms who was less popular.
findings.evidence_quote: This year’s generic ballot is right where you’d expect it to be based on the recent trendline.

findings.statement: The generic ballot sometimes takes a while to lock in: the poor Democratic midterms of 1994, 2010 and 2014 were not clearly visible in generic ballot polling by late April.
findings.evidence_quote: Democrats had very poor midterms in 1994, 2010 and 2014, but there wasn’t really much evidence of that at this point in generic ballot polling.

findings.statement: Silver did not plan to launch the 2026 midterm model before early June, because candidates in key races and even district lines were not yet set; the work is mostly data gathering since the model was built for 2018 and 2022.
findings.evidence_quote: The work is mostly about data gathering, since I put a lot of effort into our midterm model ahead of 2018 and 2022

findings.statement: Silver expects party-brand weakness to matter less once named candidates replace generic labels, and argues the model will reflect individual race-level data, with Democrats tending to nominate fairly strong congressional candidates.
findings.evidence_quote: We’ll see what the model says based on individual-level race data

findings.statement: Silver scores his own published predictions, such as the 113 predictions for Trump's second term, for calibration and considers forecast calibration valuable in its own right; he found those predictions generally well-calibrated.
findings.evidence_quote: Generally, I found the predictions were pretty well-calibrated.

political_insights.insight: Midterms are mostly about the president and the president's party, especially when it controls all levers of government; incumbency never helped the president's party in midterms and may be becoming a disadvantage even in presidential years.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Weight presidential approval heavily in the midterm national environment.

political_insights.insight: Democratic voters' poor rating of their own party reflects anger at leadership, not despondency, and angry voters turn out; they will not defect to MAGA Republicans.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Low party favorability need not imply low turnout or vote share for the out-party.

political_insights.insight: In 2018 Democrats gained 40 House seats but lost one Senate seat, largely because of a bad map.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Chamber outcomes depend on map composition, not just national environment.

references.description: Silver Bulletin Trump approval dashboard (RV vs LV)

open_questions: How the presidential approval prior is combined with the generic ballot in FLIPR, and with what weights.
The exact smoothing settings for the generic ballot versus approval averages.
